Science. A systematic, empirical inquiry into the natural world governed by the scientific method: forming hypotheses, conducting experiments, and revising theories in light of evidence. As both a body of knowledge and a process, science emerged from the Renaissance and crystallized during the Enlightenment, fundamentally transforming human understanding of nature, society, and even knowledge itself. Philosophy of science now grapples with questions of objectivity, causation, confirmation, and the relationship between theory and reality.

The scientific method emphasizes empirical observation, reproducible experiments, and falsifiability as hallmarks of genuine scientific knowledge.

The Enlightenment elevated science as the model for rational inquiry, contrasting systematic observation with religious dogma and superstition.

Positivism took science as the only meaningful form of knowledge, attempting to apply scientific rigor to ethics, society, and metaphysics.

The scientific revolution of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, including figures like Newton and Galileo, displaced medieval philosophy with mathematical physics.

Karl Popper argued that science advances through falsification. A theory is scientific if it can be proven false; confirmation alone is not enough.

Thomas Kuhn challenged the linear progress model with paradigm shifts. Science progresses through revolutionary overthrows of existing frameworks, not gradual accumulation.

Empiricism and rationalism both contributed. Empiricism insists on sensory evidence; rationalism on logical structure and mathematical laws.

Imre Lakatos proposed research programs. Science consists of competing frameworks that evolve by protecting their core assumptions and adjusting their peripheral hypotheses.

Philosophy of science debates whether scientific truth is objective or constructed. Does science discover nature or impose frameworks upon it?

The demarcation problem asks: what distinguishes science from pseudoscience? This boundary remains philosophically contested.

Science reshaped civilization. Industrialization, medicine, technology, and modern worldviews are inseparable from scientific knowledge and method.

Science connects to the Enlightenment, the historical period in which science became the supreme form of rational inquiry. Positivism is the philosophical movement that elevated science as the model for all meaningful knowledge. Empiricism is the epistemological tradition emphasizing observation and sensory evidence as the foundation of knowledge. Reason combines reason—logic and mathematics—with empirical observation. Causality is central to scientific inquiry in seeking causal explanations for natural phenomena. Verification is central to debates about scientific confirmation and what makes a claim scientifically meaningful. The Industrial Revolution applied science to transform production, energy, and human society.
